analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale or manufacture of consumer products containing the mold inhibitor chemical DMF.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on: it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee until the Congress ended, with no vote ever taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to make, sell, or distribute any consumer product containing dimethylfumarate (DMF), a fungicide used to keep mold off furniture and shoes that caused severe skin reactions in Europe. It would have classified DMF-containing products as banned hazardous substances, enforced by consumer product safety law. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and one of its subcommittees until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially children and anyone buying upholstered furniture, footwear, or other imported goods where DMF fungicide sachets were used; the bill would keep a chemical linked to severe allergic skin reactions out of products sold in the U.S.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers buying furniture, shoes, and household goods

how_it_helps.text: It treats any consumer product containing DMF as a banned hazardous substance under the Federal Hazardous Substance Act, enforceable through the Consumer Product Safety Act.
The ban would take effect 90 days after enactment, covering manufacture, sale, and distribution in commerce, so consumers would no longer encounter DMF in goods they buy.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, importers, and retailers of furniture, footwear, and household goods that used DMF sachets, who would have had to reformulate products or change suppliers within 90 days of enactment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Furniture and footwear manufacturers and retailers

drawbacks.text: An outright ban imposes compliance and reformulation costs on manufacturers and retailers of furniture, footwear, and other goods that had used DMF as a mold inhibitor, rather than a usage standard.
The bill was never debated or amended in committee, so there was no public vetting of whether the CPSC's existing hazard authorities could address DMF without a new statutory ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — preventing allergic reactions and recalls like those seen abroad — are real but limited in scope, since DMF was already being pulled from products and the EU had banned it. The cost to manufacturers is a straightforward reformulation burden. On balance a sensible, narrow consumer-safety rule whose only real cost was that it never happened.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Jackie Speier introduced the DMF Free Act of 2009 on June 26, 2009, with Jan Schakowsky as the other original supporter.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction.
On July 7, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection — its last recorded action.
The 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011 with no further action, no committee vote, and no floor vote, so the bill died in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Product manufacturers and retailers that used DMF as a mold inhibitor were spared a ban and any reformulation costs; consumers gained nothing because DMF-treated goods could still be sold.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Retailers and manufacturers that used DMF

for.name: Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban DMF in consumer products.

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor besides the sponsor, for a total of 2 cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress expired.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 7, 2009 and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats were recorded in support and no opposition ever went on the record, because the bill never reached a hearing or vote; the partisan shape of the fight cannot be determined.

industries.industry: Furniture, footwear, and household goods manufacturers and retailers
industries.note: The bill bans selling or distributing any consumer product containing DMF, a mold inhibitor used in fungicide sachets in sofas and shoes. Manufacturers would have had to reformulate or drop DMF-treated products.
Makers of safer mold inhibitors gain a mandate for alternatives; consumers gain by not being exposed to DMF, which caused severe skin reactions in Europe and triggered product recalls.
